claim: PHD2 is predominantly expressed in Tregs over other members of the PHD family.
source: Based on the predominance of Egln1 (PHD2) expression in Tregs over other members of the PHD family, we generated a mouse strain lacking PHD2 expression in Tregs (identified as PHD2ΔTreg)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing relative expression levels of PHD family members in Tregs

claim: Selective ablation of PHD2 expression in Treg leads to a spontaneous systemic inflammatory syndrome.
source: We demonstrate herein that selective ablation of PHD2 expression in Treg (PHD2ΔTreg mice) leads to a spontaneous systemic inflammatory syndrome, as evidenced by weight loss, development of a rectal prolapse, splenomegaly, shortening of the colon, and elevated expression of IFN-γ in the mesenteric lymph nodes, intestine, and spleen.
evidence: Multiple morphological and molecular parameters were measured showing inflammatory manifestations

claim: Over 70% of PHD2ΔTreg mice developed a spontaneous inflammatory syndrome.
source: While fertile and viable, over 70% of these mice developed a spontaneous inflammatory syndrome, characterized by weight loss, episodes of anal prolapse, reduced colon length, splenomegaly, and hemorrhagic abdomen (Figure 1a–e).
evidence: Direct observation and quantification of disease incidence in the mouse cohort

claim: PHD2ΔTreg mice display weight loss compared to control mice.
source: While fertile and viable, over 70% of these mice developed a spontaneous inflammatory syndrome, characterized by weight loss, episodes of anal prolapse, reduced colon length, splenomegaly, and hemorrhagic abdomen (Figure 1a–e).
evidence: Weight measurements shown in Figure 1a demonstrate statistically significant differences

claim: PHD2ΔTreg mice develop rectal prolapse.
source: While fertile and viable, over 70% of these mice developed a spontaneous inflammatory syndrome, characterized by weight loss, episodes of anal prolapse, reduced colon length, splenomegaly, and hemorrhagic abdomen (Figure 1a–e).
evidence: Visual documentation and quantification shown in Figure 1b

claim: PHD2ΔTreg mice have reduced colon length compared to control mice.
source: While fertile and viable, over 70% of these mice developed a spontaneous inflammatory syndrome, characterized by weight loss, episodes of anal prolapse, reduced colon length, splenomegaly, and hemorrhagic abdomen (Figure 1a–e).
evidence: Colon length measurements shown in Figure 1c and 1d demonstrate statistically significant reduction

claim: PHD2ΔTreg mice develop splenomegaly.
source: While fertile and viable, over 70% of these mice developed a spontaneous inflammatory syndrome, characterized by weight loss, episodes of anal prolapse, reduced colon length, splenomegaly, and hemorrhagic abdomen (Figure 1a–e).
evidence: Spleen size shown in Figure 1c demonstrates enlarged spleens in PHD2ΔTreg mice

claim: PHD2ΔTreg mice display hemorrhagic abdomen.
source: While fertile and viable, over 70% of these mice developed a spontaneous inflammatory syndrome, characterized by weight loss, episodes of anal prolapse, reduced colon length, splenomegaly, and hemorrhagic abdomen (Figure 1a–e).
evidence: Visual documentation shown in Figure 1e

claim: PHD2 deficiency in Tregs leads to an increased number of activated CD4 conventional T cells expressing a Th1-like effector phenotype.
source: PHD2 deficiency in Tregs led to an increased number of activated CD4 conventional T cells expressing a Th1-like effector phenotype.
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing increased CD44hi CD62Llo cells and IFN-γ production

claim: Expression of innate-type cytokines Il1b, Il12a, Il12b, and Tnfa is elevated in peripheral tissues and spleen of PHD2ΔTreg mice.
source: Concomitantly, the expression of innate-type cytokines such as Il1b, Il12a, Il12b, and Tnfa was found to be elevated in peripheral (gut) tissues and spleen.
evidence: qPCR measurements shown in Figure 1j demonstrate elevated mRNA levels

claim: PHD2ΔTreg mice display enhanced sensitivity to dextran sodium sulfate-induced colitis.
source: PHD2ΔTreg mice also displayed an enhanced sensitivity to dextran sodium sulfate-induced colitis and toxoplasmosis, suggesting that PHD2-deficient Tregs did not efficiently control inflammatory response in vivo, particularly those characterized by IFN-γ production.
evidence: DSS-induced colitis experiments shown in Figure 5 demonstrate increased weight loss, reduced survival, and higher clinical scores

claim: PHD2ΔTreg mice display enhanced sensitivity to toxoplasmosis.
source: PHD2ΔTreg mice also displayed an enhanced sensitivity to dextran sodium sulfate-induced colitis and toxoplasmosis, suggesting that PHD2-deficient Tregs did not efficiently control inflammatory response in vivo, particularly those characterized by IFN-γ production.
evidence: Toxoplasma infection experiments shown in Figure 5f-k demonstrate increased weight loss and immune activation

claim: PHD2-deficient Tregs do not efficiently control inflammatory responses characterized by IFN-γ production in vivo.
source: PHD2ΔTreg mice also displayed an enhanced sensitivity to dextran sodium sulfate-induced colitis and toxoplasmosis, suggesting that PHD2-deficient Tregs did not efficiently control inflammatory response in vivo, particularly those characterized by IFN-γ production.
evidence: Multiple experimental models showing increased IFN-γ production and Th1-type inflammation

claim: Treg dysregulation in PHD2ΔTreg mice is largely prevented in PHD2-HIF2α double KOs.
source: Further analysis revealed that Treg dysregulation was largely prevented in PHD2-HIF2α (PHD2-HIF2αΔTreg mice), but not in PHD2-HIF1α (PHD2-HIF1αΔTreg mice) double KOs, suggesting an important and possibly selective role of the PHD2-HIF2α axis in the control of Treg function.
evidence: Comparison of multiple mouse strains shown in Figure 6 demonstrates phenotypic rescue in double KOs

claim: Treg dysregulation in PHD2ΔTreg mice is not prevented in PHD2-HIF1α double KOs.
source: Further analysis revealed that Treg dysregulation was largely prevented in PHD2-HIF2α (PHD2-HIF2αΔTreg mice), but not in PHD2-HIF1α (PHD2-HIF1αΔTreg mice) double KOs, suggesting an important and possibly selective role of the PHD2-HIF2α axis in the control of Treg function.
evidence: Comparison of multiple mouse strains shown in Figure 6 demonstrates lack of phenotypic rescue in PHD2-HIF1α double KOs

claim: The PHD2-HIF2α axis plays an important and possibly selective role in the control of Treg function.
source: Further analysis revealed that Treg dysregulation was largely prevented in PHD2-HIF2α (PHD2-HIF2αΔTreg mice), but not in PHD2-HIF1α (PHD2-HIF1αΔTreg mice) double KOs, suggesting an important and possibly selective role of the PHD2-HIF2α axis in the control of Treg function.
evidence: Differential rescue of phenotype in double knockout strains

claim: The STAT1 pathway is a target of the PHD2-HIF2α axis in regulatory T cell phenotype and in vivo function.
source: Finally, the transcriptomic analysis of PHD2-deficient Tregs identified the STAT1 pathway as a target of the PHD2-HIF2α axis in regulatory T cell phenotype and in vivo function.
evidence: RNA-seq analysis and IPA prediction shown in Figure 8 identify STAT1 as upstream regulator

claim: CD4+ regulatory T cells account for approximately 5–10% of total circulating CD4+ T cells.
source: CD4+ regulatory T cells (Tregs), accounting for approximately 5–10% of total circulating CD4+ T cells, represent a critical subset of T lymphocytes involved in immune homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field

claim: Tregs contribute to immune tolerance to self-constituents and to mucosal antigens derived from the commensal microflora and food.
source: Through a broad set of effector mechanisms, these cells contribute to immune tolerance to self-constituents and to mucosal antigens derived from the commensal microflora and food (Lu et al., 2017; Xing and Hogquist, 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Tregs participate in the resolution of inflammatory responses.
source: Tregs also participate in the resolution of inflammatory responses (Dominguez-Villar and Hafler, 2018) and play an important role in maternal immunotolerance against the semi-allogeneic fetus (Samstein et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Tregs play an important role in maternal immunotolerance against the semi-allogeneic fetus.
source: Tregs also participate in the resolution of inflammatory responses (Dominguez-Villar and Hafler, 2018) and play an important role in maternal immunotolerance against the semi-allogeneic fetus (Samstein et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Excessive activation of Tregs impedes adequate immune responses to tumors and pathogens.
source: While critical to maintain tissue integrity, excessive activation of Tregs impedes adequate immune responses to tumors and pathogens, suggesting a tight control of their suppressive activity and tissue localization (Togashi et al., 2019; Aandahl et al., 2004; van der Burg et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Regulatory T cells are uniformly characterized by the expression of the lineage-specific Foxp3 transcription factor.
source: Although uniformly characterized by the expression of the lineage-specific, Foxp3 transcription factor (Lu et al., 2017), regulatory T cells display a wide range of phenotypic and functional properties that allow them to migrate to specific sites and suppress a variety of immune reactions, including inflammatory (Caridade et al., 2013) and humoral responses (Clement et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Regulatory T cells display a wide range of phenotypic and functional properties.
source: Although uniformly characterized by the expression of the lineage-specific, Foxp3 transcription factor (Lu et al., 2017), regulatory T cells display a wide range of phenotypic and functional properties that allow them to migrate to specific sites and suppress a variety of immune reactions, including inflammatory (Caridade et al., 2013) and humoral responses (Clement et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: The mechanisms whereby Tregs antagonize the activity of immune effectors are largely paracrine in nature.
source: Although diverse, the mechanisms whereby Tregs antagonize the activity of immune effectors are largely paracrine in nature (Vignali et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Short-range suppressive mechanisms of Tregs include competition for nutrients and/or growth factors.
source: Short-range suppressive mechanisms include competition for nutrients and/or growth factors (mostly cytokines), secretion of immunosuppressive factors, and direct, contact-mediated, inactivation of antigen-presenting cells (Wardell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Short-range suppressive mechanisms of Tregs include secretion of immunosuppressive factors.
source: Short-range suppressive mechanisms include competition for nutrients and/or growth factors (mostly cytokines), secretion of immunosuppressive factors, and direct, contact-mediated, inactivation of antigen-presenting cells (Wardell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Short-range suppressive mechanisms of Tregs include direct, contact-mediated, inactivation of antigen-presenting cells.
source: Short-range suppressive mechanisms include competition for nutrients and/or growth factors (mostly cytokines), secretion of immunosuppressive factors, and direct, contact-mediated, inactivation of antigen-presenting cells (Wardell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Tregs have to adapt to multiple lymphoid and nonlymphoid environments and suppress immune responses in a context and tissue-dependent fashion.
source: These findings suggest that Tregs have to adapt to multiple lymphoid and nonlymphoid environments and suppress immune responses in a context and tissue-dependent fashion (Shevyrev and Tereshchenko, 2019; Panduro et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Oxygen tension varies according to tissues and pathophysiological states.
source: Because oxygen tension varies according to tissues and pathophysiological states (Ast and Mootha, 2019), cells need to adapt to fluctuations in oxygen availability in order to maintain an adequate functional and metabolic status.
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Low-oxygen availability (hypoxia) plays a critical role in the pathophysiology of many immune disorders.
source: Of note, low-oxygen availability (hypoxia) plays a critical role in the pathophysiology of many immune disorders (McKeown, 2014; Bartels et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Inflammation reduces oxygen availability to tissues by affecting microvascular form and function.
source: Inflammation, in particular, is thought to reduce oxygen availability to tissues by affecting microvascular form and function, and through the recruitment of highly oxygen-consuming inflammatory cells producing NADPH oxidase-derived reactive oxygen species (Nanduri et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Inflammation reduces oxygen availability to tissues through the recruitment of highly oxygen-consuming inflammatory cells producing NADPH oxidase-derived reactive oxygen species.
source: Inflammation, in particular, is thought to reduce oxygen availability to tissues by affecting microvascular form and function, and through the recruitment of highly oxygen-consuming inflammatory cells producing NADPH oxidase-derived reactive oxygen species (Nanduri et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Reduced oxygen levels are directly sensed by a family of oxygen-dependent prolyl hydroxylases (PHD encoded by Egln gene, comprising three members).
source: In particular, reduced oxygen levels are directly sensed by a family of oxygen-dependent prolyl hydroxylases (PHD encoded by Egln gene, comprising three members) (Hirota, 2020), although other mechanisms mediated by oxygen-sensitive histone lysine demethylases (KDM) and the cysteamine dioxygenase/N-degron pathway have been recently uncovered (Baik and Jain, 2020).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) represent the best-described substrates of PHDs.
source: Hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs), a set of evolutionary conserved transcriptional regulators, represent the best-described substrates of PHDs.
evidence: This is well-established knowledge in the field

claim: HIFs are heterodimers composed of a HIFα subunit whose stability is directly controlled by oxygen availability and a constitutively expressed HIF1β subunit.
source: These factors are heterodimers composed of a HIFα subunit whose stability is directly controlled by oxygen availability and a constitutively expressed HIF1β subunit (also known as ARNT) (Wang and Semenza, 1995).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Three members of the HIFα family have been identified: HIF1α, HIF2α, and HIF3α.
source: Following the initial characterization of the first member of HIFα family (HIF1α), two additional members, HIF2α and HIF3α, have been identified and shown to be similarly regulated by O2 availability and bind to HIF1β (Webb et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: In normoxia, PHDs catalyze the prolyl-hydroxylation of HIFα subunits.
source: In normoxia, PHDs, whose affinity for oxygen is low and comparable to atmospheric concentrations, catalyze the prolyl-hydroxylation of HIFα subunits (Semenza, 2001).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Prolyl-hydroxylation of HIFα subunits allows recognition and ubiquitination by the E3 ubiquitin ligase Von Hippel–Lindau protein (pVHL) and subsequent degradation by the proteasome.
source: This post-translational modification allows recognition and ubiquitination of HIFα subunits by the E3 ubiquitin ligase Von Hippel–Lindau protein (pVHL) and subsequent degradation by the proteasome (Maxwell et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: In hypoxia, nonhydroxylated alpha subunits escape degradation and translocate to the nucleus where they bind to constitutively expressed and stable beta subunits to constitute an active heterodimer able to regulate gene expression.
source: In hypoxia, nonhydroxylated alpha subunits escape degradation and translocate to the nucleus where they bind to constitutively expressed and stable beta subunits to constitute an active heterodimer able to regulate gene expression.
evidence: This is well-established knowledge in the field

claim: HIF1α appears as ubiquitously expressed in all metazoans.
source: In particular, while HIF1α appears as ubiquitously expressed in all metazoans, HIF2α represents a late acquisition of vertebrates, displaying a more restricted tissue expression pattern (Talks et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: HIF2α represents a late acquisition of vertebrates, displaying a more restricted tissue expression pattern.
source: In particular, while HIF1α appears as ubiquitously expressed in all metazoans, HIF2α represents a late acquisition of vertebrates, displaying a more restricted tissue expression pattern (Talks et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: HIF1α and HIF2α bind to similar sequence motifs (hypoxia response elements [HREs]) and regulate the expression of a shared set of genes.
source: Although these factors bind to similar sequence motifs (hypoxia response elements [HREs]) and regulate the expression of a shared set of genes, both HIF1α and HIF2α-specific gene targets have been identified in multiple tissues (Downes et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2007; Bono and Hirota, 2020).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Both HIF1α and HIF2α-specific gene targets have been identified in multiple tissues.
source: Although these factors bind to similar sequence motifs (hypoxia response elements [HREs]) and regulate the expression of a shared set of genes, both HIF1α and HIF2α-specific gene targets have been identified in multiple tissues (Downes et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2007; Bono and Hirota, 2020).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: HIF1α expression favors the development of highly glycolytic inflammatory Th17 cells.
source: Accordingly, HIF1α expression favors the development of highly glycolytic inflammatory Th17 cells, while inhibiting the development of Tregs, which rely mostly on aerobic metabolism (Shi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: HIF1α expression inhibits the development of Tregs, which rely mostly on aerobic metabolism.
source: Accordingly, HIF1α expression favors the development of highly glycolytic inflammatory Th17 cells, while inhibiting the development of Tregs, which rely mostly on aerobic metabolism (Shi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: HIF1α plays a direct role in Th17 development through the transcriptional activation of Rorc.
source: HIF1α also plays a direct role in Th17 development, through the transcriptional activation of Rorc (Dang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Hypoxia decreases IFN-γ production of Th1-like cells in a HIF1α-dependent fashion.
source: Hypoxia decreases IFN-γ production of Th1-like cells in a HIF1α-dependent fashion (Shehade et al., 2015), while sustained expression of this transcription factor in normoxia (as observed in mice lacking PHDs expression; Clever et al., 2016) leads to an increase in IFN-γ-secreting CD4+ T cells.
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Sustained expression of HIF1α in normoxia leads to an increase in IFN-γ-secreting CD4+ T cells.
source: Hypoxia decreases IFN-γ production of Th1-like cells in a HIF1α-dependent fashion (Shehade et al., 2015), while sustained expression of this transcription factor in normoxia (as observed in mice lacking PHDs expression; Clever et al., 2016) leads to an increase in IFN-γ-secreting CD4+ T cells.
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Expression of HIF1α can be upregulated in normoxia by TCR signaling.
source: Of note, expression of HIF1α can be upregulated in normoxia both by TCR (Lukashev et al., 2001) and cytokine-initiated signals (Dang et al., 2011), confirming that HIF1α may play a role in Th1 cells development both in hypoxia and normoxia.
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Expression of HIF1α can be upregulated in normoxia by cytokine-initiated signals.
source: Of note, expression of HIF1α can be upregulated in normoxia both by TCR (Lukashev et al., 2001) and cytokine-initiated signals (Dang et al., 2011), confirming that HIF1α may play a role in Th1 cells development both in hypoxia and normoxia.
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: HIF1α deficiency improves Treg cell development, possibly a consequence of the limited requirement for glycolysis of this cell subset.
source: As previously discussed, HIF1α deficiency improves Treg cell development, possibly a consequence of the limited requirement for glycolysis of this cell subset (Shi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Hypoxia promotes Foxp3 expression in a HIF1α-dependent fashion.
source: However, hypoxia promotes Foxp3 expression in a HIF1α-dependent fashion (Ben-Shoshan et al., 2008) and expression of HIF1α is required for adequate regulatory T cell function (Clambey et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Expression of HIF1α is required for adequate regulatory T cell function.
source: However, hypoxia promotes Foxp3 expression in a HIF1α-dependent fashion (Ben-Shoshan et al., 2008) and expression of HIF1α is required for adequate regulatory T cell function (Clambey et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: HIF2α is an important mediator of Treg function in vivo.
source: Similarly, a recent report has identified HIF2α as an important mediator of Treg function in vivo, further stressing the important role of these hypoxia-induced factors in the control of in vivo inflammatory manifestations (Hsu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: PHD proteins play a role in the differentiation of peripheral (but not thymic-derived) Tregs.
source: In agreement with these conclusions, PHD proteins have also been shown to play a role in the differentiation of peripheral (but not thymic-derived) Tregs (Clever et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: PHD proteins redundantly regulate Th1 vs. iTreg development, mostly by limiting the accumulation of HIF1α.
source: Expression of these proteins appears to redundantly regulate Th1 vs. iTreg development, mostly by limiting the accumulation of HIF1α.
evidence: Inference from cited studies on PHD proteins

claim: ShRNA-mediated knockdown of PHD2 expression in Foxp3-expressing cells led to a systemic inflammatory syndrome characterized by mononuclear cell infiltration in several organs.
source: ShRNA-mediated knockdown of PHD2 expression in Foxp3-expressing cells (PHD2-KD Tregs) led to a systemic inflammatory syndrome characterized by mononuclear cell infiltration in several organs.
evidence: Supported by cited reference (Yamamoto et al., 2019)

claim: PHD2-KD Tregs displayed reduced suppressive capacities both in vitro and in vivo.
source: PHD2-KD Tregs displayed reduced suppressive capacities both in vitro and in vivo, suggesting an important and intrinsic role of PHD2 in this cell subset.
evidence: Supported by cited reference (Yamamoto et al., 2019)

claim: Loss of HIF2α expression reversed the phenotype of mice bearing PHD2-KD Tregs.
source: Of interest, loss of HIF2α expression reversed the phenotype of these mice bearing PHD2-KD Tregs, suggesting an important role of the PHD2-HIF2α axis in regulating Treg function.
evidence: Supported by cited reference (Yamamoto et al., 2019)

claim: PHD2ΔTreg mice displayed a strongly reduced expression of Egln1 mRNA in Tregs.
source: These mice displayed a strongly reduced expression of Egln1 mRNA in Tregs, while retaining control level expression of this enzyme in other, non-Treg spleen and peripheral lymph node cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: PHD2ΔTreg mice retain control level expression of Egln1 in non-Treg spleen and peripheral lymph node cells.
source: These mice displayed a strongly reduced expression of Egln1 mRNA in Tregs, while retaining control level expression of this enzyme in other, non-Treg spleen and peripheral lymph node cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Upregulation of GLUT1 expression was only found in Foxp3-expressing cells in PHD2ΔTreg mice.
source: Upregulation of GLUT1 expression, a well-known target of HIF1α, was also only found in Foxp3-expressing cells in these mice, further supporting the selective depletion of PHD2 in Tregs vs. T convs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: PHD2ΔTreg mice are fertile and viable.
source: While fertile and viable, over 70% of these mice developed a spontaneous inflammatory syndrome, characterized by weight loss, episodes of anal prolapse, reduced colon length, splenomegaly, and hemorrhagic abdomen (Figure 1a–e).
evidence: Direct observation of mouse viability and breeding

claim: The hemorrhagic abdomen in PHD2ΔTreg mice is most likely due to an increased blood hematocrit associated with an elevation in vascular permeability.
source: This last feature is most likely due to an increased blood hematocrit (with enhanced numbers of circulating red blood cells) associated to an elevation in vascular permeability, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
evidence: Hematological analysis and Evans blue vascular permeability assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The frequency of CD4+ and CD8+ conventional T lymphocytes in several lymphoid organs was not significantly altered in PHD2ΔTreg mice.
source: Although the frequency of CD4+ and CD8+ conventional T lymphocytes (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3 for gating strategy) in several lymphoid organs was not significantly altered in PHD2ΔTreg mice (Figure 1f), the total number of CD4+ cells was increased in the peripheral lymphoid organs of these mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1f

claim: The total number of CD4+ cells was increased in the peripheral lymphoid organs of PHD2ΔTreg mice.
source: Although the frequency of CD4+ and CD8+ conventional T lymphocytes (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3 for gating strategy) in several lymphoid organs was not significantly altered in PHD2ΔTreg mice (Figure 1f), the total number of CD4+ cells was increased in the peripheral lymphoid organs of these mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: Conventional T cells from PHD2ΔTreg mice displayed clear signs of spontaneous activation, as evidenced by increased expression of CD44.
source: Moreover, these lymphocytes displayed clear signs of spontaneous activation, as evidenced by the significant increase in the expression of markers (i.e., CD44) associated to an effector-like phenotype (Figure 1g and h).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1g and h

claim: Conventional T cells from PHD2ΔTreg mice have an increased capacity to produce IFN-γ.
source: Confirming these findings, intracellular staining of short-term stimulated T cells (using pharmacological agents bypassing TCR signaling) revealed an increased capacity of conventional T cells from PHD2ΔTreg mice to produce IFN-γ, while retaining control-like production of IL-17 (Figure 1i).
evidence: Intracellular cytokine staining shown in Figure 1i

claim: Conventional T cells from PHD2ΔTreg mice retain control-like production of IL-17.
source: Confirming these findings, intracellular staining of short-term stimulated T cells (using pharmacological agents bypassing TCR signaling) revealed an increased capacity of conventional T cells from PHD2ΔTreg mice to produce IFN-γ, while retaining control-like production of IL-17 (Figure 1i).
evidence: Intracellular cytokine staining shown in Figure 1i

claim: Flow cytometric analysis revealed an increased frequency of Treg cells in the spleen, lymph nodes, and lamina propria of PHD2ΔTreg mice when compared to control animals.
source: Much to our surprise, flow cytometric analysis of lymphoid organs from naive animals revealed an increased frequency of Treg cells in the spleen, lymph nodes, and lamina propria of PHD2ΔTreg mice when compared to control animals (Figure 2a).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2a

claim: Analysis of thymic cell suspensions revealed an accumulation of the Foxp3low pre-Tregs in PHD2ΔTreg mice.
source: Analysis of thymic cell suspensions revealed an accumulation of the Foxp3low pre-Tregs and a reduction in the number of mature Tregs in PHD2-deficient, Foxp3-expressing cells, suggesting an early role for PHD2 in the generation of thymic-derived Tregs (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2b and c

claim: Analysis of thymic cell suspensions revealed a reduction in the number of mature Tregs in PHD2-deficient, Foxp3-expressing cells.
source: Analysis of thymic cell suspensions revealed an accumulation of the Foxp3low pre-Tregs and a reduction in the number of mature Tregs in PHD2-deficient, Foxp3-expressing cells, suggesting an early role for PHD2 in the generation of thymic-derived Tregs (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2b and c

claim: PHD2 plays an early role in the generation of thymic-derived Tregs.
source: Analysis of thymic cell suspensions revealed an accumulation of the Foxp3low pre-Tregs and a reduction in the number of mature Tregs in PHD2-deficient, Foxp3-expressing cells, suggesting an early role for PHD2 in the generation of thymic-derived Tregs (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing altered thymic Treg development

claim: PHD2-deficient, Foxp3-expressing cells retained higher expression of CD24.
source: Accordingly, PHD2-deficient, Foxp3-expressing cells retained higher expression of CD24 (Figure 2d), a marker associated to a thymic immature state (Owen et al., 2019), further confirming a putative role for PHD2 in the development of thymic-derived Tregs.
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2d

claim: CD24 is a marker associated with a thymic immature state.
source: Accordingly, PHD2-deficient, Foxp3-expressing cells retained higher expression of CD24 (Figure 2d), a marker associated to a thymic immature state (Owen et al., 2019), further confirming a putative role for PHD2 in the development of thymic-derived Tregs.
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: No difference in the relative frequency of Treg subsets identified by the co-expression of Foxp3 with either naive and memory markers was noted in PHD2ΔTreg mice.
source: No difference in the relative frequency of Treg subsets identified by the co-expression of Foxp3 with either naive and memory markers (Figure 2e) or with master transcription factors T-bet, GATA3, or RORγt (Figure 2f) was noted in these mice.
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2e

claim: No difference in the relative frequency of Treg subsets identified by the co-expression of Foxp3 with master transcription factors T-bet, GATA3, or RORγt was noted in PHD2ΔTreg mice.
source: No difference in the relative frequency of Treg subsets identified by the co-expression of Foxp3 with either naive and memory markers (Figure 2e) or with master transcription factors T-bet, GATA3, or RORγt (Figure 2f) was noted in these mice.
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2f

claim: Splenic PHD2-deficient Tregs showed a slight, but statistically significant, reduction in the expression of Foxp3.
source: The phenotype of splenic, PHD2-deficient Tregs was however significantly altered, showing a slight, but statistically significant, reduction in the expression of Foxp3 (Figure 2g), accompanied by reduced expression of the CD25, ICOS, and CD44 markers and enhanced expression of PD-1 (Figure 2h).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2g

claim: Splenic PHD2-deficient Tregs showed reduced expression of CD25, ICOS, and CD44 markers.
source: The phenotype of splenic, PHD2-deficient Tregs was however significantly altered, showing a slight, but statistically significant, reduction in the expression of Foxp3 (Figure 2g), accompanied by reduced expression of the CD25, ICOS, and CD44 markers and enhanced expression of PD-1 (Figure 2h).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2h

claim: Splenic PHD2-deficient Tregs showed enhanced expression of PD-1.
source: The phenotype of splenic, PHD2-deficient Tregs was however significantly altered, showing a slight, but statistically significant, reduction in the expression of Foxp3 (Figure 2g), accompanied by reduced expression of the CD25, ICOS, and CD44 markers and enhanced expression of PD-1 (Figure 2h).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2h

claim: Neither CTLA-4 nor Il10 expression was altered in PHD2-deficient Tregs.
source: Of note, neither CTLA-4 (Figure 2h) nor Il10 (Figure 2i) expression was altered in PHD2-deficient Tregs.
evidence: Flow cytometry and qPCR data shown in Figure 2h and 2i

claim: Culture of CD4+ T conv from PHD2ΔTreg mice led to a consistently higher yield of Foxp3-expressing cells when activated in the presence of Treg-inducing cytokines.
source: In keeping with in vivo observations, culture of CD4+ T conv from PHD2ΔTreg mice led to a consistently higher yield of Foxp3-expressing cells when activated in the presence of Treg-inducing cytokines (Figure 2j and k).
evidence: In vitro Treg differentiation assay shown in Figure 2j and k

claim: In vitro-induced Tregs from PHD2ΔTreg mice displayed control level expression of Foxp3.
source: In contrast to their in vivo counterparts, these induced Tregs displayed control level expression of Foxp3 (Figure 2l).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2l

claim: Heterozygous Foxp3cre/+ Egln1fl/fl mice did not display any sign of inflammation or hematological dysfunction.
